Coronectomy: Why Leaving the Tooth Root Behind is Safer for Deep Wisdom Teeth

Extracting a lower wisdom tooth can sometimes carry an increased risk of nerve irritation if the tooth roots lie extremely close to the inferior alveolar nerve. In these complex structural situations, performing a coronectomy is often a much safer surgical alternative. This precise clinical procedure involves removing only the crown portion of the wisdom tooth while safely leaving the healthy, deeply embedded roots untouched in the jawbone. Over time, the remaining root structure naturally seals over and becomes safely incorporated into the surrounding bone without causing infection or pain. This protective technique successfully prevents permanent nerve damage while encouraging stable Muco-integration of the healing gum tissue above the surgical site. Standard digital dental X-rays are excellent diagnostic tools, but they only provide a flat, two-dimensional view of your complex oral structures. You might also notice a slight, painless discoloration of a single tooth or a recurring bump on your gums that mimics a pimple. Pregnancy and Oral Health Go Hand in Hand

Pregnancy brings a wave of hormonal changes that naturally increase blood flow to your gums, making them much more sensitive to plaque irritation. This often leads to a common condition known as pregnancy gingivitis, characterized by tender, swollen, or bleeding gums. Leaving these symptoms unmanaged can affect your overall well-being and disrupt the healthy Muco-integration of tissues supporting your teeth. Is Dry Mouth Affecting Your Oral Health?

A persistent dry mouth is much more than a minor inconvenience—it can actively compromise your overall dental health. Saliva acts as your mouth's natural defense mechanism, continuously washing away loose food particles, neutralizing harmful bacterial acids, and delivering essential minerals to strengthen your enamel. When your saliva production drops due to dehydration, stress, age, or specific medications, bacteria can multiply rapidly. This imbalance significantly raises your risk of rapid tooth decay, chronic bad breath, and severe gum inflammation that disrupts healthy Muco-integration. Why Teeth Shift Over Time

It is a common misconception that your teeth remain permanently locked in place after growth stops. In reality, teeth naturally move and shift throughout adulthood due to a process called mesial drift, where your teeth slowly migrate toward the front of your mouth. Everyday habits, minor bone loss from aging, tooth loss, and the gradual wear of your enamel all apply subtle, continuous pressures that alter your dental alignment over time. Keeping your gums firmly attached and maintaining healthy Muco-integration around your teeth is essential to slowing down this natural shifting process and protecting your structural stability.
